issues.issue: The preamble subscribes to "shares of" the CI Term Trust without stating a number, class or price, leaving the quantum of the subscription to be supplied from the signature page.

The acknowledgment of receipt of the Confidential Memorandum sits beside the entire-agreement clause in Section 9(b), which limits the contract to this document while Section 5(b) makes the Memorandum a document relied upon.
The Declaration of Trust is only "available upon request" and is incorporated "as amended from time to time," so the version binding the Subscriber under Section 3 is not fixed.
Terms such as "Fair Market Value" and "Affiliate" used in Sections 4 and 7 are given meaning only by an unattached Declaration of Trust, so their content must be proved from outside the document.
The incorporation of outside definitions is in tension with the entire-agreement clause in Section 9(b), which states this Agreement is the entire agreement of the Subscriber and the Trust.
The subscription is "irrevocable" yet is for shares "as set forth on the signature page," which in the executed document specifies no number or amount of Shares.

This gives acceptance to the "sole discretion of the Trustee," while Section 10 says acceptance occurs "only upon execution and delivery of this Subscription Agreement by the Trust," leaving who accepts unsettled.
Wholesale adoption of the Declaration of Trust's terms sits uneasily with the entire-agreement clause in Section 9(b) limiting the parties' agreement to this instrument.

Shareholder status is conditioned on "payment in full of the subscription price," a term the Agreement never fixes; Section 4 speaks instead of a contribution equal to collateral received and Section 8(b) of a "purchase price."

The contribution is "equal to the amount received as collateral for any securities loans," which does not say whether it means collateral outstanding at a moment, cumulative collateral, or each receipt as it occurs.
"Fair Market Value" is defined only in the unattached Declaration of Trust and the Subscriber is bound by the Trustee's valuation without stated standard or challenge mechanism.

The "qualified purchaser" representation is framed under the Investment Company Act, while Section 5(g) states the Trust is not registered under and confers no benefit of the 1940 Act, raising a question about the point of the representation.
The disclaimer of reliance on a "financial advisor" is difficult to square with Section 5(i), in which the Subscriber approves the Trustee's provision of investment management services to the Trust.

The clause simultaneously says the Subscriber relies "solely" on this Agreement, the Confidential Memorandum and "any additional documents furnished or made available by the Trustee," an open-ended category that makes the scope of the non-reliance disclaimer indeterminate.

The non-reliance language conflicts with the entire-agreement clause in Section 9(b), which confines the parties' agreement to this Subscription Agreement while this provision treats extrinsic documents as relied upon.
The Subscriber's review is measured only "to the extent the Subscriber deems necessary," a self-referential standard that gives the representation no fixed content.
The list "any sale, or the solicitation of any sale, or any Shares to it" is garbled: the final item lacks a governing noun, so what the Subscriber represents it has not paid for is unclear.

A flat statement of no intention to dispose of Shares sits against Section 5(g)'s express recognition of "rights of redemption under the Declaration of Trust," leaving redemption's status under this representation unclear.

The disclaimer that the Subscriber gets no 1940 Act benefit or protection is in tension with the Section 5(a) representation that the Subscriber is a "qualified purchaser" as defined in Section 2(a)(51) of that Act.

The Subscriber must hold "for an indefinite period of time, subject to its rights of redemption under the Declaration of Trust," so the extent of any right to get out depends entirely on an extrinsic document.

Transfers require the Trustee's consent in its sole discretion, while Section 5(g)/(h) frame the restriction as one arising from securities-law exemptions and the Declaration of Trust, leaving the true limit on transfer to be reconciled.
